title: A truth universally acknowledged
questionStemHtml: Based on the text, the 'truth universally acknowledged' is best understood as reflecting which of the following?
passageHtml: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife. However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

taskRubric.canonicalTask: Work out what the passage implies about who actually holds the supposedly universal belief.
requiredIdeas: recognize that the answer must be inferred from the narrator's framing rather than stated directly
acceptableVariants: figure out what the narrator suggests about the so-called truth
determine whose belief this really is
commonWrongTasks: state the main idea of the whole novel
decide whether the man really wants a wife

processingUnits.textHtml: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
requiredIdeas: a wealthy single man is said to need a wife
the claim is framed as a truth everyone accepts
prohibitedDistortions: the man himself announces that he wants a wife

processingUnits.textHtml: However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.
requiredIdeas: the man's own feelings and views may be entirely unknown
the surrounding families are nonetheless convinced and treat him as a future husband for one of their daughters
requiredRelations: contrast between the man's unknown views and the families' fixed conviction
prohibitedDistortions: the families consult the man about his intentions
the man has agreed to marry someone

passageRubric.canonicalSummary: The narrator announces, as if it were a universal truth, that a rich single man must want a wife — then reveals that the conviction really lives in the minds of the neighbouring families, who treat any such newcomer as belonging to one of their daughters regardless of his own unknown views.
requiredIdeas: the opening claim is framed as universally accepted
the surrounding families are the ones who hold and act on the belief
the man's own feelings are unknown and effectively ignored
requiredRelations: contrast between the stated universal truth and the families' self-interested conviction
the families' belief leads them to regard the newcomer as destined for one of their daughters
prohibitedDistortions: the man himself declares he wants a wife
the narrator sincerely endorses the claim as literal fact

preanswerRubric.canonicalPreanswer: The 'truth' is really the expectation of the neighbouring families: they, not the man, believe a wealthy bachelor must marry one of their daughters.
requiredIdeas: the belief belongs to the families or community rather than to the man himself
acceptableVariants: it is the neighbours' assumption projected onto the newcomer
the families' hopes, presented ironically as a universal truth
prohibitedClaims: the man has said he wants to marry
the narrator literally believes all rich men seek wives

choices.label: A
choices.html: The sincere conviction of wealthy single men that they ought to marry promptly.
choices.rationaleHtml: The passage stresses that the man's feelings and views are unknown — the conviction belongs to the families, not to him.

choices.label: B
choices.html: The expectations of families hoping to see a wealthy newcomer married to one of their daughters.
choices.rationaleHtml: Correct. The second sentence locates the 'truth' in the minds of the surrounding families, who treat the newcomer as intended for one of their daughters whatever his own views.

choices.label: C
choices.html: The narrator's belief that marriage is the only reliable source of happiness.
choices.rationaleHtml: The passage never discusses happiness; this adds a claim the text does not make.

choices.label: D
choices.html: A legal obligation binding men of fortune to marry within their neighbourhood.
choices.rationaleHtml: 'Rightful property' is figurative; reading it as a legal rule takes the irony literally and infers far beyond the text.
